summary: The note explains carbon neutrality, the EU's commitment to reach it by 2050 through the European Climate Law, and its link to the Paris agreement's 1.5-degree goal. It defines carbon sinks and sequestration, notes natural sinks and their limits, and describes carbon offsetting tools such as the ETS and the carbon border adjustment mechanism. It closes with the EU's 2030 target of at least a 55% emissions cut and the Fit for 55 legislation package.
one_line: Explains carbon neutrality, the EU's binding 2050 climate-neutrality goal, carbon sinks, offsetting tools and the Fit for 55 package.
key_facts: The European Green Deal was presented by the European Commission in December 2019 as its flagship plan to make Europe climate neutral by 2050.
The EU's commitment to carbon neutrality by 2050 is set into binding EU legislation through the European Climate Law.
Limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, which the IPCC suggests is safe, requires carbon neutrality by the mid-21st century.
The Paris agreement was signed by 195 countries, including the EU.
Article 4 of the Paris agreement calls for a balance between anthropogenic emissions by sources and removals by sinks of greenhouse gases in the second half of this century.
A carbon sink is any system that absorbs more carbon than it emits; the main natural carbon sinks are soil, forests and oceans.
According to estimates, natural sinks remove between 9.5 and 11 gigatonne of CO2 per year.
Annual global CO2 emissions reached 37.8 gigatonne in 2021.
No artificial carbon sinks are currently able to remove carbon from the atmosphere on the necessary scale to fight global warming.
Carbon stored in natural sinks such as forests is released through forest fires, changes in land use or logging.
Carbon offsetting means offsetting emissions made in one sector by reducing them somewhere else, for example through investment in renewable energy or energy efficiency.
The EU's emissions trading system (ETS) is an example of a carbon offsetting system.
The EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism would apply carbon prices on imported goods from less climate ambitious countries.
The European Parliament and Council adopted the Climate Law in 2021, making the 2050 climate-neutrality goal legally binding.
The EU's interim emission reduction target for 2030 was updated from 40% to at least 55%.
The Fit for 55 legislative package includes rules on emissions trading, national emissions reduction targets, carbon removal in the land use sector and transport emissions.
